title: The Kadambawa Men and the Dream
title_raw: THE KADAMBAWA MEN AND THE DREAM
notes:
In Indian Nights' Entertainment (Swynnerton), p. 348, a weaver girl
said to herself that it would be a good thing if she married in her own
village, but if she had a son and he were to die, how her relatives
and friends would lament! The thought of it made her cry. When her
aunts and friends observed it they all cried too, and her father and
uncles and brothers coming up and seeing all these people crying,
also cried. When a neighbour asked the men what it was about, who was
dead? they could not tell him, but referred him to the women. He then
learnt that these also did not know, but cried because they saw the
girl crying.
text:
When some Kadambawa men, having joined together, were going away to
Puttalam, it became night while they were on the road. Having got a
resting-place, and cooked and eaten, while they were sleeping a tusk
elephant appeared to a man in a dream.

On the morning of the following day the man said to the other men,
"Friends, last night I saw an evil dream."

The men asked, "What was in the dream?"

The man said, "I saw a tusk elephant."

Then the men began to interpret the dream. They said, "What is the
meaning? If there is a tusk elephant there will be elephant's dung;
if elephant's dung, paddy [which the elephant has eaten]; if paddy,
uncooked rice; if uncooked rice, cooked rice; if cooked rice, it is
a thing [found only] in the village. Therefore the elephant means
the village. Something must have happened. It is useless for us to
go on. Let us go back to the village." So all, weeping and weeping,
set out to return to the village.

As they came to the rice field of the village, the women and boys of
the village having heard the men coming crying and crying aloud, said,
"Ane! Our men are coming crying and crying. What is it? It will be a
dreadful thing." So the women and boys, having come from the houses to
that side of the field before those men came across, began to cry also.

On seeing them, the man who saw the dream said to those other men,
"Look there! Did I tell you falsely?" Then the men cried the
more. Having seen it, these boys and women, they also cried more
and more. The two parties having come quite near each other still
cried. The women and boys on that side of the stile [at the edge of
the field], these men on the field side of it, except that they cried
said nothing.

While they were crying and crying until it became night, as a man
from another village was going along the path he heard this uproar,
and came to see what it was. He asked at the hand of the men, "What
is it? Who is dead?"

Then the men, crying and crying, said, "Who is dead we don't know."

After that, the man having gone near those women and boys, asked,
"What is it? Who is dead?"

Then those persons also said, crying and crying, "Who is dead we
don't know."

Afterwards the man having stopped the crying of both parties, when he
had asked them about it, there was nothing dreadful. So the man went
away, and these men and women and boys, they also went to their houses.

カダンバワの男たちが連れ立ってプッタラムへ出かけたとき、道中で夜になった。休む場所を得て、煮炊きして食べ、眠っているあいだに、一人の男の夢に牙のある象が現れた。
翌朝、その男はほかの男たちに言った。「友よ、ゆうべ悪い夢を見た」
男たちが尋ねた。「どんな夢だ?」
その男は言った。「牙のある象を見た」
そこで男たちは夢解きを始めた。そして言った。「どういう意味だ。牙のある象がいれば象の糞がある。象の糞があれば〔象が食べた〕籾がある。籾があれば生米がある。生米があれば炊いた飯がある。炊いた飯といえば、村に〔しか〕ないものだ。だからこの象は村のことだ。何か起きたにちがいない。先へ行っても甲斐がない。村へ引き返そう」。そこで一同は泣きながら泣きながら、村へ帰ろうと出発した。
村の田まで来ると、村の女たちや子どもたちが、男たちが大声で泣きながら来るのを聞いて言った。「アネ! うちの男たちが泣きながら来る。何ごとだろう。恐ろしいことにちがいない」。そこで女たちや子どもたちは、男たちが田を渡ってくる前に家から田のこちら側へ出てきて、やはり泣きはじめた。
それを見て、夢を見た男はほかの男たちに言った。「見ろ! おれが嘘を言ったか?」 すると男たちはいっそう泣いた。それを見て、子どもたちも女たちもいっそうますます泣いた。二組はすぐ近くまで来てもなお泣いていた。女たちと子どもたちは〔田の端の〕踏み越し段の向こう側、男たちは田の側にいて、泣くばかりで何も言わなかった。
夜になるまで泣きに泣いていると、別の村の男が道を通りかかってこの騒ぎを聞きつけ、何ごとかと見に来た。男は男たちに尋ねた。「どうした? 誰が死んだのだ?」
すると男たちは泣きながら言った。「誰が死んだのかはわからない」
そのあと男は女たちと子どもたちのそばへ行って尋ねた。「どうした? 誰が死んだのだ?」
するとこの者たちもまた泣きながら言った。「誰が死んだのかはわからない」
そのあと男が両方の泣くのをやめさせて事情を尋ねてみると、恐ろしいことは何もなかった。そこで男は去っていき、男たちも女たちも子どもたちも、みな家へ帰った。
